units.title: RAG retrieves passages first, then generates from them
units.claim: A RAG system answers in two stages: it retrieves passages from a collection, then a language model writes the answer from those passages.
units.explanation: The frame for everything else: each later section is one part of the retrieval stage or its hand-off to generation.

omission.reason: Without it the pipeline has no starting point.

units.title: The answer can be no better than what retrieval returns
units.claim: The model never sees the rest of the collection, so the answer can only be as good as the retrieved passages.
units.explanation: The main claim of the document. It is why the rest of the note is about retrieval and why reranking can't rescue a missed passage.
mustPreserve: never sees the rest of the collection

units.title: BM25 finds exact terms and rare identifiers
units.claim: Keyword retrieval (BM25) scores passages by the query terms they contain, weighting rare terms higher; it is cheap, needs no training and finds exact strings such as E-4012 or sync.retry_window even when they occur once.
units.explanation: The lexical signal and its strength.

units.title: BM25 misses passages that use different words
units.claim: Keyword retrieval's weakness is vocabulary mismatch: 'why does my upload stall' does not match a passage that only says 'transfers pause when the connection drops'.
units.explanation: The limit of the lexical signal; it belongs on the BM25 card.

units.title: Embeddings find passages that mean the same thing
units.claim: Vector retrieval encodes the query and passages as embeddings and returns the closest ones, so passages with the same meaning are found even when they share no words.
units.explanation: The semantic signal and its strength, the complement of BM25's weakness.

units.title: Embeddings are weak on exact codes
units.claim: Embeddings are weaker on exact codes and identifiers: E-4012 and E-4021 look almost the same to the encoder, and vector retrieval alone missed the correct passage for 31 of 50 error-code queries.
units.explanation: The limit of the semantic signal, with its evidence; it belongs on the vector card.

units.title: Changing the encoder means a 6-hour re-embedding
units.claim: Embeddings must be recomputed whenever the encoder changes, which takes about 6 hours for this collection.
units.explanation: An operational cost of vector retrieval.

omission.reason: Operational detail; not part of the retrieval argument.

units.title: Hybrid search merges both retrievers' lists and can improve recall
units.claim: Hybrid search runs both retrievers on the same query and merges their result lists, which can improve recall.
units.explanation: The central design move. The claim is a possibility, never a guarantee.

paraphrase.note: 'can improve' must not become 'improves' or 'always improves'.

units.title: Only when the signals are complementary
units.claim: The gain depends on the signals being complementary, each retriever finding relevant passages the other misses; if both return the same passages or one is poorly tuned, merging adds latency without adding much.
units.explanation: The condition on ku.hybrid. Dropping it turns a conditional benefit into an unconditional one.

units.title: Scores on different scales are fused by rank
units.claim: BM25 scores and vector similarities are on different scales and can't be added, so Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) ignores raw scores and uses only each passage's rank in each list.
units.explanation: Why RRF, and what it uses.

units.title: RRF sums 1/(k + rank) with k = 60
units.claim: Each passage receives 1/(k + rank) from every list it appears in, the contributions are summed, and k = 60; a larger k flattens the difference between top and lower ranks.
units.explanation: The protected formula and constant.

paraphrase.note: The formula and the value of k are exact.

units.title: Candidate generation is tuned for recall
units.claim: Each retriever returns its top 50 passages, so the fused list holds at most 100 candidates; this stage aims to get the right passage somewhere in the list, not first.
units.explanation: The hand-off between retrieval and reranking, and its goal (recall over precision).

units.title: 50 per retriever, not 100
units.claim: Raising the limit to 100 per retriever found the right passage slightly more often but roughly doubled reranking time, so the limit stayed at 50.
units.explanation: A design decision with its reason.

omission.reason: Supporting detail of the candidate stage.

units.title: A cross-encoder rescores the fused candidates and keeps the top 8
units.claim: A cross-encoder reads the query and one passage together and outputs one relevance score, judging relevance far more accurately than either retriever; it is too expensive for the whole collection, so it runs only on the fused candidates, and the top 8 passages are kept.
units.explanation: The reranking step: what it is, why it runs only on candidates, and what it hands on.

units.title: Reranking improves the precision of the top results
units.claim: Reranking improves the precision of the top results.
units.explanation: What reranking buys. Always shown with its limit (ku.rerank-limits).

units.title: …but it can't make the answer correct or recover a missed passage
units.claim: Reranking does not guarantee a correct answer: it can only reorder what retrieval found, so a right passage missing from the candidates can't be recovered, and a relevant passage may still be out of date.
units.explanation: The critical limitation of the reranking claim. It must sit on the same card.
mustPreserve: can only reorder what retrieval found

units.title: The model answers only from the top 8 passages and cites them
units.claim: The language model gets the question and the top 8 passages, answers only from them, cites the passages it used, and says so when none addresses the question instead of answering from general knowledge.
units.explanation: The end of the pipeline and its fallback rule.
mustPreserve: say so when none addresses the question

units.title: Citations don't show whether a passage is current
units.claim: Citations let a reader check each claim against its passage, but do not show whether the passage itself is current.
units.explanation: A limit on the citation part of ku.generation.

omission.reason: May be dropped with care; if shown it sits on the generation card.

units.title: Example: 'What does E-4012 mean?' needs both signals
units.claim: For 'What does E-4012 mean?', BM25 retrieves the error-code table, vector search the article on resumable uploads, and the reranker keeps both in the top 8, so the answer can define the code and explain the fix.
units.explanation: Illustrates the whole pipeline, and complementary signals in particular. Supporting, not a main idea.

related.note: A case where the signals are complementary.

units.title: Each stage buys relevance with latency and cost
units.claim: On 400 test questions the correct passage reached the top 8 for 61% (BM25 only, 35 ms, $0.02 per 1,000 queries), 68% (vector only, 60 ms, $0.10), 79% (hybrid RRF, 70 ms, $0.12) and 88% (hybrid + reranker, 190 ms, $0.95).
units.explanation: The measured trade-off. A table is the natural element.

paraphrase.note: Numbers stay exact; keep the four configurations.

units.title: Reranking adds about 120 ms per query
units.claim: Reranking adds about 120 ms per query, mostly running the cross-encoder over up to 100 candidates, and accounts for most of the cost increase.
units.explanation: The price of reranking's precision.

units.title: The figures come from one collection and one query set
units.claim: These figures come from one collection and one query set; a collection with fewer exact identifiers may gain less from BM25, and a different reranker will have a different latency.
units.explanation: Qualifies the latency (and the table). Belongs with the latency claim.

units.title: A tight latency budget can rerank fewer candidates
units.claim: With a strict latency budget, rerank fewer candidates, for example the top 30 of the fused list, at some cost in recall.
units.explanation: An option, conditional on a latency budget, with its own cost.

units.title: Each step helps only under its own conditions
units.claim: Hybrid search widens the net, reranking sorts the catch and generation can only work with the passages it is given; each step helps only under its own conditions and none makes the answer certain to be right.
units.explanation: The takeaway, with its own limit.

mustNotClaim.why: The source says it can improve recall when the signals are complementary, and adds latency for little gain otherwise.
The source says explicitly that it does not.

mustNotClaim.claim: Reranking improves recall / finds passages retrieval missed.
mustNotClaim.why: The reranker can only reorder the candidates; it cannot recover a passage that isn't among them.

mustNotClaim.claim: Generation feeds back into retrieval (or the reranker depends on the answer).
mustNotClaim.why: The pipeline runs one way: retrieval → fusion → reranking → generation.

mustNotClaim.claim: The measured gains (88%, 120 ms) hold for any collection or reranker.
mustNotClaim.why: The source limits the figures to one collection and one query set.
